row.title: Round the Yule-Log: Christmas in Norway
row.author: Peter Christen Asbjornsen

plot_extraction.response_text:
A newly commissioned lieutenant, recovering from fever and stranded alone in Christiania on Christmas Eve, expects to miss the holiday with his family. His elderly landladies invite him to join their small gathering, where he, the children, and several older women exchange folktales about trolls, brownies, and ghosts. The evening ends cheerfully with Christmas food and good wishes, but the supernatural stories, rich supper, and his weakened condition give the lieutenant a restless night filled with bizarre dreams.

He awakens to find Thor, his father’s servant, standing over him with a letter, a fur coat, and the welcome news that a horse is waiting outside. His father has sent Thor to bring him home if he is well enough to travel. Overjoyed, the lieutenant leaves the city by sledge and returns to his family’s house, where he receives a jubilant welcome and enjoys an exceptionally happy Christmas.

style_extraction.response_text:
The story adopts the manner of a nineteenth-century Christmas reminiscence, combining domestic realism, urban antiquarianism, oral folklore, gentle comedy, and restrained supernatural horror. Its frame is intimate and autobiographical: a first-person narrator looks back on his youth as a newly commissioned lieutenant, recovering from illness and stranded in Christiania on Christmas Eve. The retrospective voice is genial, observant, and lightly self-mocking. Although the narrator begins in loneliness and “black” spirits, his melancholy never becomes psychologically severe; it mainly prepares the emotional contrast between isolation, fireside companionship, nocturnal unease, and the final joyful return home.

The narrative has a pronounced frame-tale structure. The opening establishes the narrator’s circumstances and the old-fashioned household, after which the action becomes a communal storytelling session. A sequence of embedded folktales—about brownies, trolls, Peter Gynt, and a congregation of the dead—occupies most of the story. These tales are introduced through conversation and attributed to distinct speakers, preserving the sense that folklore passes from servant to mistress, parent to child, and one generation to another. The frame resumes near the end, when the stories mingle in the narrator’s feverish dream before ordinary reality breaks in with the arrival of his father’s servant. Structurally, the movement is circular and restorative: the narrator begins separated from home and ends travelling back to it.

The prose is descriptive, leisurely, and strongly atmospheric. Exterior scenes rely on wintry visual and auditory details: whistling wind, sweeping snow, black sky, dark façades, sledge-bells, and lamplit windows. Interiors are rendered through firelight, old furniture, portraits, deep rooms, passages, garrets, and heavy architectural features. The physical setting does more than provide background; it creates a credible habitat for inherited superstition. The old house, with its gloomy staircases and ghostly associations, harmonises with the age and habits of the landladies, while the Christmas setting makes the transition from ordinary domestic life to folklore feel natural.

Diction is formal and period-specific, with spellings and expressions such as “cosey,” “countenances,” “by my troth,” “gude-wife,” and “Lor’ bless and preserve us.” Social titles—“Lieutenant,” “Madame,” “Miss,” and “Mother”—are used frequently and help establish a ceremonious, hierarchical world. The vocabulary often has an antiquarian flavour, especially in descriptions of buildings, clothes, furniture, and customs. At the same time, the embedded tales use plainer, more repetitive language, conventional formulas such as “once upon a time,” and colloquial exclamations. This contrast distinguishes the educated narrator’s polished recollection from the oral style of nursery and household storytelling.

Sentence structure tends toward long, coordinated or subordinated sentences containing qualifications, digressions, and accumulations of detail. Semicolons, dashes, and commas sustain a conversational flow, while periodic sentences allow descriptions or anecdotes to unfold gradually. The narrators within the story frequently interrupt themselves to correct uncertain details—whether an event happened on a Thursday or Christmas Eve, where someone lived, or what a forgotten name was. These hesitations imitate spontaneous speech and lend the tales an air of oral authenticity. Repetition is also important: phrases such as “tell us,” “Christmas Eve,” and “the brownie” create rhythm, reinforce the communal setting, and reproduce the eager insistence of children.

Dialogue is abundant and theatrical. Characters are differentiated less through deep interior analysis than through speech habits, gestures, and recurring physical details. The children speak in excited choruses, using emphatic repetitions and direct emotional declarations. Miss Mette and Miss Cicely are courteous and old-fashioned; Mother Skau is blunt, sceptical, garrulous, and bodily comic, punctuating her stories with coughing, choking, and pinches of snuff. Thor’s rural speech is direct and repetitive, especially when he reports the father’s instructions. These voices give the piece the quality of a performed fireside gathering rather than a private literary meditation.

The handling of the supernatural is deliberately ambiguous. Within the inset tales, brownies, trolls, and ghosts are treated as factual presences, but the frame narrative does not confirm their objective reality. Stories are repeatedly supported by chains of hearsay—someone knew a servant who saw a brownie, or a truthful mother had witnessed evidence—yet the speakers also admit uncertainty and contradiction. Humour tempers fear: trolls mistake a bear for a cat, brownies are tricked into noisy houses, and frightened children discover that their own raised legs have caused the sensation of being touched. Even the narrator’s climactic encounter with the peasant from his dream receives a natural explanation. The style therefore preserves the imaginative force of folklore without requiring firm belief in it.

Tone shifts fluidly between nostalgia, amusement, suspense, and warmth. The brownie stories are mischievous and earthy, often ending with violence presented as comic justice. The church story is quieter and more genuinely uncanny, using pallor, silence, recognition, and the torn cloak to intensify dread. The narrator’s subsequent dream turns that fear into grotesque comedy when his dead grandfather somersaults from the pulpit and calls for a dance. This tonal modulation prevents the story from becoming either solemnly supernatural or merely farcical. Its dominant mood is affectionate nostalgia for old customs, old houses, local legends, and communal Christmas life.

Pacing is slow and expansive in the opening description, episodic through the central sequence of tales, briefly accelerated during moments of supernatural danger, and swift in the concluding journey home. The repeated pattern of invitation, story, audience reaction, and request for another tale creates a cumulative fireside rhythm. The final section resolves the frame rapidly, with the father’s servant arriving, the mare carrying the narrator through good roads, and the family home appearing almost as the fulfilment of a Christmas wish.

The story’s imagery depends heavily on contrasts: darkness and firelight, cold streets and warm rooms, sickness and restored health, solitude and company, fear and laughter, the dead congregation and the living family. Food functions as a recurring emblem of domestic abundance and supernatural exchange. Christmas porridge may appease a brownie, stolen delicacies provoke punishment, troll feasts become grotesque parodies of human celebration, and the landladies’ cakes, jellies, wine, porridge, and pork restore ordinary cheer. The closing homecoming completes this movement from deprivation to nourishment and belonging.

Overall, the style is that of a folkloric Christmas tale presented through a polished memoiristic frame. Its defining features are an avuncular first-person narrator, detailed antiquarian settings, long conversational sentences, vivid character dialogue, nested oral narratives, comic treatment of superstition, carefully moderated ghostly suspense, and a sentimental but controlled conclusion. The prose values sociability and inherited tradition above plot economy: its central pleasure lies in hearing different voices tell old stories while winter and darkness gather outside.

generation.response_text:
### A Christmas Eve in the Old House

It is now more than forty years since the Christmas of which I am about to speak; yet, whenever the first snow lies blue in the twilight, and the bells of a passing sledge are heard beyond the windows, I see again the narrow streets of old Christiania, the black gables, the lamps swinging in the wind, and one illuminated pane upon which I looked with exceedingly little Christian resignation.

I was then a newly commissioned lieutenant, and possessed, besides my sword, a pair of epaulettes of which I was secretly vain, a moustache scarcely visible except in strong sunshine, and that cheerful confidence in my own consequence which belongs to the age of twenty-one. Unfortunately, I had also possessed a fever. It had left me pale, weak in the knees, and subject to such sudden changes of spirits that in the morning I regarded life as a glorious campaign, while by four o’clock I was prepared to believe myself abandoned by mankind.

My father’s house lay nearly seven Norwegian miles from the town. I had intended to go home three days before Christmas, but the regimental surgeon, who had a heart of iron where young officers were concerned, forbade the journey.

“You may eat,” said he, “but not too much; drink, but very little; walk, but not far; sleep, if you can; and, above all, remain where you are.”

He then went away to dine with a family at Aker, leaving me to practise these negative virtues alone.

I lodged in an ancient house which stood in a street now so altered that I should hesitate to point out the spot. The lower storey was of stone, with small arched windows; the upper was built of dark timber, bulging outward as though it had grown weary of standing upright. A gateway, strong enough for a fortress, opened upon a paved yard, where an old pump, two wood-sheds, and a pear-tree of fabulous age maintained a melancholy existence. There were deep rooms, crooked passages, unexpected steps, presses built into the walls, and a garret extending over the whole house, full of broken spinning-wheels, worm-eaten chests, portraits without names, and names without portraits.

My landladies, Miss Mette and Miss Cicely Hagerup, were sisters, both advanced in years, though each spoke of the other as “the elder one.” They had caps like small snowdrifts, black silk mittens, and countenances which united benevolence with a certain ceremonious dignity. Miss Mette was tall and moved slowly; Miss Cicely was round, quick, and perpetually losing her spectacles. They had inhabited the house since the reign of King Christian VII, and seemed to me scarcely less a part of it than the carved chimney-piece or the Dutch tiles around the stove.

Christmas Eve came with a north-west wind. Snow swept along the street in white smoke; the sky darkened before three; doors banged, bells rang, servants hurried past with baskets, and every window appeared to promise the happiness denied to me. I had received no letter from home. The post had been delayed, the roads were said to be heavy, and I pictured my father, mother, sisters, brothers, dogs, horses, servants, and even the old red cow, assembled without me.

I sat at my window in a military cloak, though the stove was hot, and indulged in those black reflections which are most impressive when one is young, convalescent, and certain of an audience in one’s own breast.

At half-past five there came a gentle knock.

“Enter!” I cried, in a tone intended to indicate that sorrow had made me stern.

Miss Cicely put her cap around the door.

“Lieutenant,” said she, “my sister and I cannot permit you to remain alone upon Christmas Eve.”

“You are very kind, Miss Cicely; but I fear I should be poor company.”

“Then you will suit us perfectly, for we are all poor company until supper.”

She disappeared before I could frame another objection; and presently Miss Mette entered, carrying a wax candle.

“You must come,” she said. “The children are here, and Mother Skau, and my cousin Madame Lange. We have porridge, cakes, a little wine, and a pork roast which Cicely declares is too large, though I consider it scarcely respectable. Put on your better coat, Lieutenant. Christmas Eve should not find a man sulking in his chamber.”

There was no resisting this. Ten minutes later I followed her through the passage to the best parlour.

The room made a picture which has remained in my memory when many scenes of greater magnificence have vanished. A fire burned upon the hearth; candles stood before the mirror and upon the old square piano; red apples, nuts, and small gilt baskets hung upon a fir-tree in the corner; and over the polished table was spread a cloth white enough, as Miss Cicely afterward observed, to put the snow to shame. The walls bore portraits of deceased Hagerups—pastors, magistrates, merchants, and one captain who had gone down with his vessel off Jutland, though, to judge from his portrait, no storm should have had courage to approach him.

Three children belonged to Madame Lange: Elise, aged eleven; Henrik, aged nine; and little Andreas, who had reached six, but denied it whenever the statement appeared likely to deprive him of a privilege. Madame Lange herself was a mild widow with smooth hair and a voice which made even reproof sound apologetic.

Mother Skau, who was neither our mother nor, so far as I know, any Skau’s mother, sat close to the stove. She had once been nurse in the Hagerup family, and was now a stout, red-cheeked old woman, wrapped in so many shawls that she resembled a parcel sent from the country. On the table beside her stood a snuff-box, a glass of currant wine, and a saucer containing sugared almonds, all three of which she visited in regular order.

“Here is the Lieutenant!” cried the children.

“Not so loud,” said Madame Lange.

“Let them shout,” said Mother Skau. “Noise keeps away what ought not to come. Sit here, Lieutenant, where I can see whether the fever has left your eyes. H’m! Pale as candle-grease, but that may be the uniform.”

I sat down among them; and before many minutes had passed, the children, who possessed the blessed art of regarding every grown man under thirty as a possible conspirator, had persuaded me to cut paper soldiers, mend a wooden horse, and hide three nuts in my pockets for purposes which were never explained.

Outside, the wind cried in the chimney. The old house responded with creaks, taps, and long sighs from distant passages. There was no sound which Miss Mette could not attribute to shrinking timber, nor any which Mother Skau could not attribute to something less natural.

“That was the garret door,” said Elise, when a dull blow shook the ceiling.

“The garret door is bolted,” replied Miss Mette.

“Then,” said Mother Skau, taking snuff, “it is some one who does not require doors.”

The children drew closer.

“Tell us a story,” said Henrik.

“No,” said Madame Lange.

“Yes,” said Andreas.

“Not a frightening one,” Madame Lange added.

“A very frightening one,” said Elise.

“And one that is true,” Henrik insisted.

“All good stories are true in one place or another,” observed Mother Skau.

Miss Cicely, who had found her spectacles upon her own forehead, folded her hands.

“Perhaps,” said she, “we might begin with the house-brownie. There is nothing alarming in a brownie if he is properly treated.”

“There is,” said Mother Skau, “if he is not.”

The children turned at once to Miss Cicely, and she began.

“My grandmother’s father—I believe it was her father, though it may have been her uncle—owned a farm in Gudbrandsdal. The farm was called Lower Hov, unless it was Upper Hov; but that does not signify, for the brownie knew the difference even if I do not. He lived in the barn, behind the great beam, and was no higher than Andreas there.”

“I am high,” said Andreas.

“So was the brownie, for his kind. He wore a grey jacket, red cap, leather breeches, and wooden shoes. No one saw him often, but every one saw his work. If a cow loosened herself in the night, he tied her again; if the horses lacked hay, he pulled it from the loft; and if a lazy servant left the stable dirty, the brownie flung the broom after him in the morning.”

“Did it hurt?” asked Henrik.

“If the servant deserved it.”

“That is not an answer,” said Henrik.

“It is the best answer you will get in this world,” said Mother Skau.

Miss Cicely continued. “On Christmas Eve a bowl of porridge, with a large piece of butter in the middle, was always set for him in the barn. One year the dairymaid, who was a careless girl—Karen, or Maren, or perhaps Anne—”

“She has begun badly,” Mother Skau remarked.

“—put the butter at the bottom of the bowl, thinking it made no difference. The brownie came after midnight, tasted the porridge, and found no butter. He was so angry that he went into the cowshed and struck the best cow dead.”

“Oh!” cried Elise.

“He then returned, ate deeper, and found the butter. At once he was filled with remorse. ‘I have been hasty,’ said he. ‘The gude-wife did not forget me after all.’ So he went to the neighbouring farm, took their best cow, and brought it back to replace the one he had killed.”

“That was stealing,” said Henrik.

“Brownies,” said Miss Cicely, “have an imperfect understanding of property.”

“And did the neighbour come for his cow?” asked Andreas.

“He did; but the brownie seized him by his belt and hung him upon the weathercock until morning.”

Madame Lange looked doubtful. “Cicely, you said there was nothing alarming in it.”

“Nothing at all, my dear. The man was taken down and lived for years.”

“Crooked,” added Mother Skau. “He was crooked ever afterward, if it is the same story.”

“It may not be.”

“It is always the same story,” said Mother Skau, “only the farm changes.”

The children laughed, and even Madame Lange consented to smile. A gust of wind scattered snow against the panes like a handful of dry peas.

“Tell another brownie story,” said Elise.

“One which you know yourself,” said Henrik.

“Nobody knows a brownie story himself,” said Miss Mette. “That would require being older than is convenient.”

Mother Skau inhaled so heroic a pinch of snuff that speech became impossible for nearly a minute. She coughed, waved away assistance, drank currant wine, coughed again, and at last announced that she knew a tale upon the word of a woman incapable of falsehood.

“She was a cook at a place near Drammen,” Mother Skau began, “and the brownie there was a little black fellow, hairy about the arms, with eyes like two sparks under a kettle. He was civil to those who were civil to him; but he could not abide quarrelling.

“Now, the farmer and his wife quarrelled from breakfast until bedtime. If he said the sun shone, she fetched an umbrella; if she said the porridge was hot, he put on his mittens. The brownie bore it for seven years. Then, on the eighth Christmas Eve, while they were shouting over a dish of sausages, he came down from the loft with his red cap over one ear.

“‘I am leaving,’ said he.

“‘Good riddance!’ cried the farmer.

“‘Take the cat with you!’ cried the wife.

“The brownie made no reply, but carried his little chest to a farm two miles distant. The servant who drove the cart had gone scarcely half-way when he heard a voice from inside the chest:

“‘How far have we come?’

“‘As far as the mill bridge,’ said the servant.

“Then a tiny voice under the cart answered:

“‘I am coming too.’

“It was the other brownie—the brownie of the new farm—hanging underneath by his fingers.

“‘Lor’ bless and preserve us!’ cried the servant. ‘Then there will be two brownies where there should be one.’

“‘No,’ said the first. ‘You take my place, and I shall take yours.’

“So they exchanged farms. But the brownie who went to the quarrelsome house lasted only three days. On the fourth morning both brownies met upon the bridge, each carrying his chest.

“‘Can you endure them?’ asked one.

“‘No,’ said the other. ‘Can you?’

“‘No.’

“They sat upon the railing and considered. At last they agreed to return together and cure the farmer and his wife. That night, when the quarrel began, one brownie took the husband by the hair, the other took the wife by the heels, and they beat them together like two rugs until neither had breath to speak.

“After that there was peace in the house.”

“Were they killed?” asked Andreas.

“Not at all. They had eleven children afterward.”

“That,” Madame Lange said, “is not a story I should have chosen.”

“But it contains a moral,” replied Miss Mette.

“All beatings contain morals when other people receive them,” said Mother Skau.

At this point Miss Cicely brought round a plate of thin cakes flavoured with aniseed. We ate, and the old clock in the corner struck seven, pausing so long between the strokes that Andreas counted nine. The fire settled with a soft crash; shadows moved behind the high-backed chairs, and the painted captain over the piano appeared to advance one polished boot from his frame.

“Now trolls,” said Henrik. “Brownies are too small.”

“Yes, trolls!” cried Elise. “A great one with three heads.”

“Seven,” said Andreas.

“Three is more probable,” observed Miss Mette.

“Nothing about trolls is probable,” said Madame Lange.

“That is why they are worth hearing about,” I ventured; and, having now forgotten both my loneliness and my fever, I offered to relate a story told to me by Thor, my father’s old servant.

The children composed themselves at once.

“Once upon a time,” I began, “there was a charcoal-burner named Halvor, who lived at the edge of a forest with his wife, a white goat, and a yellow dog. Whether he had children I cannot say; Thor put in two when he told the story on Sunday and took them out again on Monday. Halvor was poor, but he owned a gun, a sledge, and an old brown bear which he had captured as a cub.”

“People do not own bears,” said Henrik.

“This man did. He had named it Bishop.”

“Why?”

“Because it sat solemnly and disliked being disturbed at dinner.

“One Christmas Eve Halvor set out to carry the bear to a gentleman who wished to buy it. Snow came on heavily, and when darkness fell he saw a light at a farmhouse. The farmer stood at the door wringing his hands.

“‘Can I lodge here?’ asked Halvor.

“‘You may,’ replied the farmer, ‘but you will get neither food nor rest. Every Christmas Eve a company of trolls comes down from the mountain. They eat our supper, drink our ale, break the furniture, pinch the servants, and dance on the roof. We are leaving before they arrive.’

“‘I shall remain,’ said Halvor, ‘if I may put Bishop under the stove.’

“The farmer agreed, and fled with his household. Halvor chained the bear in the kitchen, lay down behind the woodpile, and waited.

“At midnight the door burst open. In came the trolls: tall trolls, short trolls, trolls with noses like ladles, trolls with tails like ropes, and one old troll-wife whose three heads contradicted one another. They filled the room and demanded Christmas fare. One emptied the porridge-pot; another swallowed the ham whole; a third drank ale from the butter churn.”

Andreas sighed with admiration.

“Presently the smallest troll saw the bear’s nose sticking from under the stove.

“‘Oh, what a pretty cat!’ he cried. ‘May I feed it sausage?’

“Before any one could stop him, he thrust a forkful against Bishop’s nose. The bear sprang out, broke its chain, and seized the troll by the breeches. The troll screamed; the three-headed wife screamed in three different keys; and the entire company rushed for the door. Bishop followed them across the yard, scattering trolls into snowdrifts, trees, and the frozen duck-pond.

“The next Christmas Eve, as the farmer stood in his doorway, he heard a voice call from the mountain:

“‘Does your great cat still live?’

“‘Yes!’ shouted the farmer. ‘And she has seven kittens, each twice as large as herself!’

“‘Then we shall not come!’ cried the troll; and none ever did.”

Andreas clapped. Elise declared that she had heard the same story, but with a polar bear; Henrik maintained that the farmer’s assertion about the kittens was a lie and ought not to have succeeded.

“It was a military stratagem,” I told him.

Miss Mette nodded graciously. “That makes it quite respectable.”

Mother Skau, however, sniffed. “Trolls are not so easily cheated.”

“You have known some?” I asked.

“I have known people with worse manners.”

She then related, without waiting to be pressed, how a fiddler had once been carried into a mountain and compelled to play for a troll wedding. The bride was as long as a church aisle, with a silver crown and a cow’s tail hidden beneath her green gown; the bridegroom wore a red waistcoat and had moss growing from both ears. Their guests drank molten gold, ate roasted stones, and danced until sparks flew from their heels.

“The fiddler played,” said Mother Skau, “because what else could he do? He played a spring dance, a halling, and a tune which his grandfather had learned from a waterfall. At last an old troll offered him a drinking horn.

“‘Drink, little man.’

“But the fiddler suspected it was no wholesome brew. He threw the contents over his shoulder, and wherever the drops fell, the rock smoked.

“‘You have spilt my ale,’ said the troll.

“‘My hand slipped,’ said the fiddler.

“‘Then your head shall slip next.’

“Just at that moment the church bells rang for Christmas morning. The mountain split open; all the trolls shrieked and vanished; and the fiddler found himself sitting in the snow with the drinking horn in his hand. He carried it to the king’s treasury, where it remains.”

“Have you seen it?” asked Henrik.

“I have seen a horn.”

“Was it that one?”

“They said it was.”

“Who said?”

“A man at the door.”

Henrik shook his head with the severity of a judge. Mother Skau rewarded his scepticism by pinching his ear.

Miss Mette now suggested a song, perhaps because Madame Lange had begun to look anxiously at the children. We sang two verses of a Christmas hymn. Miss Cicely played the piano, missing certain notes with such confidence that they appeared to be at fault; and for a little while the room was filled with living voices instead of trolls. Yet, when the last chord died, the wind returned more loudly than before, descending through the chimney with a long, hollow murmur.

“What about Peter Gynt?” Elise asked.

“Which Peter Gynt?” said Miss Cicely.

“The hunter,” replied the child. “The one who saw the invisible beasts.”

“There have been many Peter Gynts,” Mother Skau declared. “Too many, if half their tales are true.”

Miss Mette knew one. She settled more upright in her chair and spoke with the grave precision of a person reading from an invisible family chronicle.

“Peter Gynt was a hunter who feared neither man nor beast, because, as he said, men made too much noise and beasts knew better than to attack him. One autumn evening he was crossing the mountains above Vågå. The mist lay so thick that he could not see the point of his gun. He had lost the track, his food was gone, and the night promised frost.

“As he stumbled among the stones, his foot struck something soft.

“‘Take care!’ said a voice.

“Peter stopped. He saw no one.

“‘Who are you?’

“‘I am a crooked horned buck,’ answered the voice, ‘and you have trodden upon my ear.’

“Peter felt around and found nothing. He walked on. Soon he struck another invisible body.

“‘Take care!’ cried a second voice. ‘You have kicked my grandmother.’

“‘How many of you are here?’ Peter asked.

“‘As many as the hills have stones.’

“Then the mist lifted a little, and he perceived—not with his eyes, perhaps, but with that other sight which sometimes comes to lonely travellers—that the whole mountain was covered with beasts. There were bucks as large as barns, birds with iron feathers, cats whose whiskers swept the valleys, and a serpent curled three times around the highest peak. None could be seen plainly; but the air bent around them, and their breathing rolled through the fog.

“‘Which way leads to Vågå?’ Peter called.

“A voice behind him said, ‘Straight through my left eye.’

“Another said, ‘Under my tongue.’

“A third said, ‘Between the teeth of my youngest child.’

“Peter considered. Then he took a silver button from his coat, loaded his gun with it, and fired into the air. At the shot, all the invisible beasts leaped. The mountain trembled; stones rolled down the slopes; the mist tore apart like a curtain. Peter saw the true path immediately below him.

“But one enormous creature—whether buck, bird, or serpent he never knew—followed him as far as the churchyard. He could hear its claws upon the frozen ground: click, click, click. At the gate he turned and made the sign of the cross. The sound ceased, and in the morning they found three marks upon the gatepost, burned so deep that no plane could remove them.”

“Are the marks there still?” whispered Elise.

“They were there in my grandmother’s time.”

“And now?”

“I have not lately examined the gate.”

Mother Skau nodded. “That is the way of it. Young people ask whether marks remain, but never trouble to go and look.”

I confess that Miss Mette’s quiet voice, and especially her account of the clicking claws, affected me more than the trolls. I looked toward the dark window, where my own pale reflection seemed to stand outside in the snow. My recent illness had left the nerves too ready to take alarm, though pride prevented me from admitting it.

The children, however, were delighted.

“Another!” they cried. “Tell us another! A ghost this time!”

“No ghosts,” said Madame Lange firmly.

“A little ghost,” pleaded Andreas.

“There are no little ghosts.”

“How do you know?”

Madame Lange found no immediate reply.

Miss Cicely busied herself with the candles. “There is the story of the dead congregation,” she said, apparently to no one.

Mother Skau put down her glass.

“That is no tale for children.”

“Then it must be a very good one,” said Henrik.

Madame Lange objected, but softly; the children promised not to be frightened, which is the promise children most readily make and least frequently keep; and I, who should have supported the mother, asked Miss Cicely whether the occurrence had taken place in Christiania.

“Not in the town,” she replied, “but at a little church north of here. My father knew the pastor who heard it from the sexton’s widow, and she was a woman of unimpeachable character.”

Mother Skau muttered that a good character was no defence against the dead.

Miss Cicely lowered her voice.

“Many years ago there lived near that church an old woman named Ingeborg. She was poor, but pious, and earned her bread by weaving. On Christmas Eve she sat at her loom later than was customary, for she had promised a piece of linen to the pastor’s wife. The moon shone brightly upon the snow, and the church bell struck eleven.

“Ingeborg thought it was the morning bell. The clock she possessed had stopped; she was old and tired; and, seeing light in the church windows, she supposed she had slept through the night and that the Christmas service had begun.

“She put on her cloak, took her hymn-book, and hurried across the fields. The church door stood open. Within, every candle burned, and the pews were crowded.

“At first Ingeborg was ashamed to be late. She slipped into the last pew and bowed her head. Yet something seemed strange. Though the church was full, no one coughed, moved a foot, turned a page, or whispered. The air was cold enough to show every breath, but no breath appeared.

“The pastor stood in the pulpit with his back toward her. He wore an old-fashioned ruff and a black gown powdered with dust. When he turned, Ingeborg recognised Pastor Rasmus, who had been dead twenty years.

“She looked about her. In the nearest pew sat her former mistress, dead before Ingeborg’s marriage. Beside her was the miller drowned in the spring flood; beyond him, a child buried the previous summer. All the congregation were dead.

“Ingeborg could neither rise nor cry out.

“Then a woman sitting before her turned slowly. It was Ingeborg’s godmother, who had been dead since Ingeborg was a girl.

“‘Go,’ the dead woman whispered. ‘This service is not for you.’

“Ingeborg’s hands shook so that she dropped her hymn-book.

“‘Go at once,’ said the godmother. ‘They have begun to know you.’

“Now faces were turning throughout the church—not quickly, but one after another, row after row. Their countenances were pale, their eyes fixed, and earth clung to some of their garments. The dead pastor lifted one hand.

“Ingeborg sprang up and ran.

“As she reached the porch, many cold fingers caught the back of her cloak. She heard no footsteps behind her, only the rustle of grave-clothes and the turning of hundreds of heads. The cloak held. She tore herself free, crossed the churchyard, and fell senseless at her own door.

“In the morning they found her there. When the sexton unlocked the church for the true service, a strip of her cloak lay inside the door; and every shred had been torn as if by many hands.”

No one spoke when Miss Cicely finished. The room had become very still. Even the fire appeared to listen.

Little Andreas had drawn both feet up upon his chair. Suddenly he gave a sharp scream.

“Something touched my leg!”

Madame Lange caught him; Elise shrieked because he had shrieked; Henrik overturned a stool. Miss Mette raised the candle, and Mother Skau, after peering beneath the table, discovered that Andreas’s right foot, numbed by its position, had descended upon his left ankle.

“You are your own ghost,” she told him.

This brought such general laughter that the dead congregation withdrew at once to its proper distance. Andreas laughed loudest, though with tears still shining on his cheeks.

The parlour door opened, and the maid announced supper.

Never has a procession from fear to appetite been more rapid. We entered the dining-room, where a great bowl of rice porridge steamed upon the table. There were pork, sausages, cabbage, apples, preserved cherries, cakes of several shapes, and a jelly which trembled at every movement as though it retained the terrors we had escaped. Miss Mette gave us each a spoonful of porridge; Miss Cicely watched to see who found the hidden almond; Mother Skau declared the pork underdone and ate three slices to prove it.

The almond came to me.

“Then the Lieutenant will be married before next Christmas!” cried Elise.

“Impossible,” said I. “I am under the surgeon’s orders.”

“Surgeons have nothing to do with it,” Mother Skau answered.

We drank a modest glass of wine to Christmas, to absent friends, and to the hope that all travellers might find open doors. At this toast I thought of home. My melancholy returned, but no longer bitterly. The kindness around me had softened it; and when Miss Mette wished health to my father and Miss Cicely health to my mother, I could only bow, for my voice failed.

At ten the children were wrapped in cloaks and comforters. Henrik carried a lantern, Elise held her mother’s hand, and Andreas, already half asleep, was borne away by the maid. Mother Skau departed in a hired sledge, shouting from beneath her shawls that we must leave porridge in the garret. The bells receded along the street.

My landladies accompanied me to my door.

“You have not passed so sad a Christmas Eve after all,” said Miss Mette.

“No,” I replied. “I shall remember it with gratitude.”

“Do not remember the church story,” said Miss Cicely. “I ought not to have told it.”

“Dream of the pork,” advised Miss Mette. “It was more substantial.”

I wished them good night and went to bed.

The advice was excellent, but impossible to follow. Whether the fever still lurked in me, whether the wine had been stronger than Miss Mette believed, or whether porridge, pork, cakes, jelly, trolls, brownies, and dead congregations should never be crowded into one invalid upon the same evening, I cannot say. I slept, but my sleep was a theatre in which every tale returned wearing the garments of the others.

First I dreamed that I sat upon the brown bear, Bishop, and rode through the streets of Christiania. He wore my epaulettes, while I had only a red brownie’s cap. At every window stood a troll eating rice porridge. Each troll had the face of the regimental surgeon and called after me, “You may ride, but not far; eat, but not much; wake, if you can!”

Then the bear carried me into a mountain where Mother Skau, with three heads and a silver crown, presided over a wedding. Miss Cicely played the fiddle; the children danced with invisible beasts; and Miss Mette walked among them asking whether it was Upper Hov or Lower Hov and finding neither answer satisfactory.

The scene changed. I stood outside the old church. Snow covered the graves, but beneath it I heard innumerable fingers scratching upward. The door opened of itself. Within sat my ancestors, dressed according to their portraits. My great-grandfather wore a wig; an aunt who had died in infancy appeared as a severe old lady; and the painted sea-captain from the Hagerups’ parlour occupied the pulpit.

He turned—and became my grandfather, who in life had been the gravest of men.

“Too late!” he cried. “The Lieutenant is too late for Christmas!”

At once every dead face turned toward me.

I tried to retreat, but cold fingers seized my cloak. The congregation rose. My grandfather leaped from the pulpit, performed a somersault with astonishing agility, and called for a dance. The organ began a wild halling. Skeletons stamped upon the pews; the drowned miller spun the troll-bride; the brownie beat time with a dead cow; and Peter Gynt flew overhead upon an invisible buck, shouting that the way home lay through its left eye.

In the midst of this uproar a peasant in a sheepskin coat pushed toward me. His beard was covered with frost; his hands were enormous; and he repeated, with dreadful persistence:

“Are you well enough? Are you well enough? Are you well enough?”

I struggled to wake, but the peasant shook me.

“Lieutenant! Lieutenant, sir! Are you well enough to travel?”

I opened my eyes.

Grey Christmas morning filled the room. The fire had died; the candle had burned into its socket; and beside my bed stood—not a dead peasant, troll, or invisible beast, but Thor, my father’s old servant, in his broad sheepskin coat.

For several seconds I stared at him.

Thor stared back, his weather-beaten countenance divided by a grin.

“Well, sir,” he said, “the master said I was to ask if you were well enough; and if you were well enough, I was to bring you; but if you were not well enough, I was not to bring you, though I was to ask the doctor; and if the doctor said—”

“Thor!”

“Yes, Lieutenant?”

“Are you real?”

He scratched his head. “I have been so until now.”

He held out a letter. Upon the chair lay my father’s great fur travelling-coat, and from the street below came the impatient ringing of sledge-bells.

The letter was brief. My father wrote that the roads had improved, that he had sent Thor with our sure-footed mare, Freya, and that, if I had no fever and felt equal to the journey, I was to come home without delay. My mother added three lines in the margin, one of my sisters had drawn six exclamation marks beneath them, and my youngest brother had written, “BRING HIM,” in capitals across the seal.

I believe I laughed like a child. I got out of bed, discovered myself far stronger than I had been the day before, and dressed while Thor repeated my father’s instructions in every possible arrangement.

Miss Mette and Miss Cicely came hurrying from their rooms, each wearing a shawl and carrying a candle.

“What has happened?” cried Miss Cicely.

“I am going home!”

They comprehended at once. There followed coffee, bread, cold pork, questions about the road, warnings against the wind, and such active rejoicing that the whole house appeared to awaken. Miss Mette wrapped a comforter around my neck; Miss Cicely slipped cakes into my pocket; both insisted that I wear my father’s fur coat over everything else.

As Thor carried down my portmanteau, Miss Cicely said, “You see, Lieutenant, the strange man who woke you had a natural explanation.”

“Entirely natural,” I replied.

“But perhaps,” Miss Mette added, “you had better not tell Mother Skau. She prefers explanations of another kind.”

The morning was pale and clear when we drove from the gateway. Snow lay over the roofs and softened the black façades; smoke rose straight from the chimneys; church bells sounded across the town, solemn yet joyful. Here and there a door opened upon children in their Christmas clothes, servants carrying baskets, or old gentlemen saluting one another with elaborate bows.

Freya trotted briskly. The runners sang upon the packed snow; Thor cracked his whip without touching the mare; and the city fell behind us.

Beyond the last houses the country opened white and shining. Pines stood laden with snow; frozen rivers wound between the hills; and every farm we passed had a little curl of smoke above it and straw set out for the birds. The air bit my cheeks, but beneath the fur coat I was warm, and with each mile I seemed to leave weakness behind.

Thor talked nearly all the way. He told me how my mother had looked from the window each time bells were heard; how my father had twice declared that no sensible man would send a convalescent over winter roads and had then ordered the sledge before daylight; how my sisters had dressed the tree but refused to light it; and how even the old dog, knowing that something was expected, slept in the entrance hall.

At noon we climbed the last ridge. There, across the white fields, stood home: the long yellow house, the dark firs behind it, the barns and stable roofs, and smoke rising from the kitchen chimney.

A figure at an upper window waved a handkerchief. Another appeared at the door. Then the door flew open, and the entire household poured out as though the house itself could no longer contain them.

My father came first, walking with dignity for perhaps six paces and then forgetting it. My mother followed without cloak or bonnet. My sisters ran past them both; my brothers shouted; the old dog bounded through the snow, barking so violently that he rolled over.

Before Freya had stopped, I was pulled from the sledge and embraced, questioned, scolded for being pale, praised for coming, and carried almost bodily into the hall. The tree was lighted that evening; the Christmas dinner was reheated with additions; every one spoke at once; and I found, beneath my plate, a paper star upon which my youngest sister had written, “For our Lieutenant, who came after all.”

Thus ended the most melancholy Christmas Eve of my youth and began, I think, the happiest Christmas Day of my life.

I have since travelled farther in worse weather, passed festivals in foreign cities, and sat at grander tables than either Miss Mette’s or my father’s. Yet no splendour has ever effaced that old parlour, with its portraits and candles, the children’s eager countenances, Mother Skau’s snuff-box, the wind in the chimney, and the kindly voices saying, “Tell us another.”

Nor, when I hear sledge-bells on a winter morning, can I altogether prevent myself from expecting the door to open upon Thor in his sheepskin coat, bearing a letter and repeating, as though the fate of kingdoms depended upon the answer:

“Are you well enough, Lieutenant? The master says, if you are well enough, you are to come home.”

The Clockmaker of Low Tide

Every morning, when the sea withdrew from Bellweather Bay, it left behind the usual things: ropes of kelp, pale shells, bottles clouded by salt, and once, to great local excitement, a wooden leg with a silver buckle.

On the morning Elias Vale found the clock, the tide had gone farther out than anyone in the town could remember.

The bay lay open beneath a colorless sky, its wet sand shining like a road of dark glass. Fishing boats rested on their sides in the harbor, exposing bellies striped with barnacles. Gulls strutted over places where waves should have been, bewildered by their sudden kingdom.

Elias was twelve years old, an age at which he was considered too young to be trusted with a boat but old enough to mend nets until his fingers bled. His father had sent him to gather driftwood before breakfast. Instead, he followed a line of footprints across the sand.

They began near the harbor wall.

This was strange, because the footprints came from the sea.

They were narrow and deep, as if made by someone carrying a heavy burden. Elias looked toward the horizon. In the distance, the water had retreated into a silver band. No person was visible. Only the footprints remained, crossing the exposed bay and ending beside a black rock.

Half buried in the sand was a clock.

It was no larger than a dinner plate. Its case was brass, green with age, and its face was covered by thick glass. There were no numbers. Instead, tiny painted images circled the dial: a cradle, a ship, a key, a rose, a knife, a crown, a grave, and dozens of other symbols too small for Elias to understand.

It had only one hand.

The hand pointed to a painted door.

Elias lifted the clock. It was surprisingly warm.

The instant his fingers closed around it, a sound came from inside the case.

Tick.

The bay trembled.

Tick.

A flock of gulls rose together, shrieking.

Tick.

Far out at sea, the silver line of water began to move.

Elias tucked the clock under his coat and ran home.

His father, Bram Vale, was in the kitchen splitting a stale loaf with a knife. He was a broad man with gray in his beard and a permanent bend in his shoulders from years spent hauling traps. Since Elias’s mother had died, he had spoken mostly in instructions.

“Wood?” Bram asked.

“I found something.”

“Unless it burns, put it away.”

Elias placed the clock on the table.

Bram’s knife stopped halfway through the loaf.

For a moment, all color left his face.

“Where did you get that?”

“On the sand.”

“Where?”

“Beyond Widow’s Rock.”

Bram seized Elias by the shoulders. “Did anyone see you?”

“No.”

“Did you wind it?”

“It was already ticking.”

Bram released him and backed away. The clock’s single hand had moved. It no longer pointed to the door.

Now it pointed to a ship.

His father snatched a flour sack from a hook, wrapped the clock in it, and shoved it into the cold ashes of the stove.

“You will not touch that again,” he said.

“What is it?”

“Nothing.”

“You know what it is.”

“I know trouble when it enters my house.”

Bram took his coat and left without eating. Through the window, Elias watched him hurry uphill toward the church.

The tide returned before noon.

It did not creep back in its ordinary way. It rushed over the sand in one great shining sheet, lifting boats, swallowing rocks, and filling the harbor almost to the top of the wall. The town bell rang a flood warning, though there was no storm. People ran from the waterfront carrying baskets, children, ledgers, cages, whatever they valued most.

Then the water stopped.

By evening the bay was calm, but unease had settled over Bellweather. Old people stood in doorways whispering. Fishermen tied extra knots in their mooring lines. The priest walked along the harbor sprinkling holy water until a wave soaked his boots.

Bram returned after dark.

“With the spring tide,” he told Elias, “you’ll go inland to your aunt.”

“But I’ve never met her.”

“She has a farm near Tor Hill.”

“I don’t want to go.”

“This is not a matter of wanting.”

“Is it because of the clock?”

Bram stared into the fire. “There is no clock.”

From inside the stove came a soft, patient ticking.

That night Elias dreamed of his mother.

He remembered very little about her when awake: dark hair threaded with copper, a laugh that arrived suddenly, hands that smelled of lavender and fish scales. In the dream she stood ankle-deep in the bay, wearing the blue dress in which she had been buried.

“You took your time,” she said.

Elias tried to run to her, but the sand clung to his feet.

“Are you dead?” he asked.

“Everyone is, somewhere.”

“I don’t understand.”

“You will.”

She pointed toward the harbor. A ship was sailing into Bellweather Bay, though no wind moved its black sails. Figures crowded its deck. Some wore crowns, some carried lanterns, and some had seaweed trailing from empty eye sockets.

At the wheel stood a woman in a red coat.

Elias woke to find the clock beside his bed.

The flour sack lay folded beneath it.

Its hand still pointed to the ship.

At dawn, a ship appeared beyond the harbor mouth.

It was small, narrow, and painted white. Its single sail was red, the brightest thing under the gray sky. It came forward without wind or oars and docked with such precision that its hull barely kissed the pier.

A woman stepped ashore.

She wore a long red coat, black gloves, and boots polished enough to reflect the clouds. Her hair was white, though her face was neither young nor old. A scar crossed her left cheek like a thin stroke of chalk.

“Good morning,” she called to the gathering townspeople. “I am looking for a clock.”

No one answered.

The woman smiled.

“Brass case. One hand. Poor manners. Has anyone seen it?”

Bram pushed through the crowd. “Leave this town.”

“Bram Vale,” she said warmly. “Still giving orders to tides?”

“You took my wife.”

“No. She made a bargain.”

“You twisted it.”

“I fulfilled it.”

Elias, watching from behind a stack of lobster pots, felt his heart strike his ribs.

The woman turned her head directly toward him.

“And there is her boy.”

Bram lunged, but two sailors stepped from the ship. They looked human except for their eyes, which were perfectly black.

“Run!” Bram shouted.

Elias ran.

He fled uphill through narrow streets, past the bakery, the schoolhouse, and the church with its green copper roof. The clock beat against his chest beneath his coat. Behind him came the tolling of the town bell.

At the northern edge of Bellweather stood the abandoned workshop of Silas Orr, the clockmaker.

Silas had disappeared seven years earlier. Some said he had fallen from the cliffs. Others said he had built a clock that could reverse death, tested it on himself, and become an infant. His workshop remained untouched because no one wanted to discover which story was true.

Elias broke a window and climbed inside.

Hundreds of clocks covered the walls. Grandfather clocks, carriage clocks, cuckoo clocks, watches, sundials, and hourglasses filled with black sand stood beneath sheets of dust. None of them moved.

At the back of the room was a desk buried under papers. Elias set down the brass clock, and every clock in the workshop began to strike.

The noise was enormous.

Bells rang. Springs shuddered. Wooden birds burst from tiny doors. Hands spun around painted faces. An hourglass flipped itself over and over until it shattered.

Then, all at once, silence returned.

A panel opened in the desk.

Inside lay a leather book bearing Elias’s family name.

He opened it.

The first pages were filled with diagrams of the brass clock. Later pages contained lists of names and dates. Some names were marked with a black wave. Others had been crossed out.

Near the end, Elias found his mother’s name.

Mara Vale — one year purchased. Price: one unclaimed hour.

Below it, in different handwriting, someone had added:

The hour cannot remain unclaimed. It will seek an owner. If the Clock of Tides returns, the debt has ripened.

The workshop door creaked open.

The woman in red stood on the threshold.

“You have her eyes,” she said.

Elias stepped back. “Who are you?”

“Captain Anja Rook.”

“What happened to my mother?”

“She was dying before you were born. Her heart was weak. The doctors said she would not survive the winter, and you would never take your first breath.”

Elias gripped the book. “My father said you took her.”

“I gave her twelve months. Enough time to bear you, name you, and hold you. In return, she promised me one hour that belonged to no living soul.”

“That makes no sense.”

“Time rarely does.”

Captain Rook removed one glove. On her palm was a circular scar shaped like the clock’s dial.

“Your mother believed there were hours no one wanted,” she continued. “Hours wasted in waiting rooms, prison cells, sickbeds. But every hour belongs to someone. Joyful or miserable, each one must be lived. So the clock took payment from the future.”

“Whose future?”

“Yours.”

The clock ticked faster.

Elias looked down. Its hand had moved beyond the ship and now pointed to a knife.

“What happens when it goes all the way around?”

“The unclaimed hour opens. For sixty minutes, all possible moments exist together. The dead may return. The unborn may speak. Lost ships enter harbor. Old wounds reopen. And when the hour ends, the clock chooses a life to erase so the balance may be restored.”

“My life?”

“Most likely.”

Captain Rook held out her scarred hand.

“Give it to me. I can carry it beyond the last line of longitude, where time has no authority.”

“Then why didn’t you do that before?”

Her expression changed, and Elias knew he had found the edge of a lie.

“Because,” she said, “the clock cannot cross the final sea without a living keeper.”

“You need me.”

“I need someone.”

Elias thought of the black-eyed sailors.

“What happened to the last keeper?”

“He became the clockmaker whose workshop you entered.”

“Silas Orr?”

“He lasted longer than most.”

A floorboard groaned overhead.

Captain Rook glanced up.

Bram dropped from the loft, a whaling harpoon in his hands. He drove it through the captain’s red coat and into the wall.

For an instant she remained pinned there, more surprised than hurt.

Bram grabbed Elias.

“Go!”

They escaped through the broken window. As they ran downhill, every door in town opened at once.

The dead came out.

An old fisherman walked from the bakery with a hook still buried in his throat. Three children who had drowned in the winter flood skipped hand in hand toward the school. A soldier in an ancient uniform stood in the square calling for a regiment buried two centuries before.

People screamed, wept, or rushed forward to embrace those they had lost.

Elias stopped.

His mother stood beside the fountain.

She wore the blue dress from his dream.

Bram saw her and staggered as if struck.

“Mara?”

She smiled.

He crossed the square slowly, unable to breathe. When he reached her, he lifted one hand but did not quite touch her face.

“You got old,” she said.

Bram laughed then, a broken sound Elias had never heard from him.

“You didn’t.”

They embraced.

For a few seconds Elias forgot the clock, the captain, and the terrible debt. He ran to them, and his mother folded him into her arms.

She smelled of lavender and fish scales.

“My little tidepool,” she whispered.

He began to cry.

The clock ticked against his chest.

His mother drew back. “You found it.”

“Captain Rook says I have to die.”

“Anja always mistakes rules for fate.”

“You knew her?”

“I knew what she was.”

“What is she?”

“A collector. A ferryman. A prisoner of her own bargain. Names matter less than choices.”

The clock’s hand moved from the knife to a painted crown. Around them, the square shifted. Buildings appeared and vanished. The church became a ruin, then a forest, then a church again. Elias saw himself as an old man standing beneath the bell tower. He saw himself drowned. He saw children with his eyes. He saw an empty place where Bellweather had once been.

“What do I do?” he asked.

His mother knelt before him.

“The clock was built to make one moment belong to no one. That is its weakness.”

“I don’t understand.”

“You will.”

She kissed his forehead and turned to Bram.

“I am sorry,” she said.

“No,” he replied. “Stay. Just until it ends.”

“I can’t.”

“You have an hour.”

“I have already spent it.”

Her body began to fade.

Bram clung to her, but his arms closed on empty air.

Across the square, Captain Rook approached. The harpoon still protruded from her chest, though no blood marked her coat. Behind her came the two black-eyed sailors.

“The hour is collapsing,” she said. “Give me the clock.”

Elias pulled it out.

The hand pointed to the grave. Only two symbols remained before the painted door where it had begun.

“What will you do with me?” he asked.

“You will board my ship. If we reach the final sea, Bellweather will be spared.”

“And me?”

“I cannot promise.”

His father stepped between them. “Take me instead.”

“The debt is not yours,” said Rook.

“Then make it mine.”

“You cannot give another person your death.”

Bram seized the clock.

The moment he touched it, the glass cracked.

A sound like thunder rolled beneath the town.

All around them, possible worlds opened.

In one, Bram lay dead in the square. In another, Captain Rook’s ship burned in the harbor. In another, Elias had never been born, and his parents walked past each other as strangers on a summer road.

The clock’s hand advanced to the final symbol: an eye.

Captain Rook tore the harpoon from her chest. “Decide now!”

Elias remembered his mother’s words.

The clock had been built to make one moment belong to no one.

Every hour belonged to someone. That was why the debt could never be paid.

Unless the hour belonged to everyone.

Elias took the clock from his father and raised it above his head.

“I claim this hour,” he said.

Nothing happened.

Captain Rook laughed bitterly. “It is already yours.”

“Then I give it away.”

“To whom?”

“To everyone.”

He hurled the clock onto the stones.

The brass case dented, but did not break.

The hand reached the painted door.

The door on the clock face opened.

It was not a picture anymore. It was a true door, impossibly small and filled with white light. From it came a wind that smelled of every season: snow, rain, hot dust, apples, chimney smoke, newborn grass.

Elias picked up a loose paving stone and struck the clock.

Once.

The glass shattered.

Twice.

The brass split.

On the third blow, the single hand snapped.

The unclaimed hour burst open.

It passed through Bellweather in a wave.

Every person in the town suddenly remembered a life they had never lived. They remembered being kings and beggars, sailors and murderers, beloved children and lonely ghosts. Each felt the first breath of birth and the last beat of death. For one boundless instant, no moment belonged to one person because all moments belonged to all.

The debt vanished.

Captain Rook screamed.

Cracks of white light spread across her skin. Her black-eyed sailors collapsed into heaps of wet rope. In the harbor, the red sail tore loose and flew upward, becoming a flock of crimson birds.

Rook reached for Elias.

“What have you done?”

“Changed the rules.”

“No one changes the rules.”

“My mother did.”

The captain’s face softened. Beneath her anger was something older and sadder: relief.

“Yes,” she whispered. “She did.”

Then the light carried her away.

The clocks in Silas Orr’s workshop began ringing on the hill. The church bell answered. Soon every bell in Bellweather was sounding, though no hand pulled any rope.

The dead disappeared.

The possible worlds closed.

The sea returned to its proper place.

Elias woke at sunset with his head in his father’s lap. The square was crowded with townspeople, all silent, all changed in ways they would struggle to explain.

In Elias’s hand lay a piece of broken brass.

It was shaped like a tiny door.

Years passed.

Bellweather rebuilt the windows shattered by the unclaimed hour, repainted the boats, and turned Captain Rook’s vanished ship into a story told on winter nights. Most people eventually decided that the tide had released a strange gas from beneath the sand, causing the entire town to dream together.

Bram Vale never agreed or disagreed.

He became gentler after that day. He still spoke in instructions, but sometimes the instructions were, “Sit down and watch the sunset,” or, “Your mother liked this song,” or, “The nets can wait until morning.”

Elias grew tall. He sailed beyond the bay, though never beyond the last line of longitude. He studied gears, springs, stars, and tides. At twenty-three, he reopened Silas Orr’s workshop.

Above the door he painted:

ELIAS VALE  
CLOCKS REPAIRED  
LOST HOURS FOUND

People brought him watches that ran slow, clocks that struck thirteen, and music boxes that had forgotten their tunes. He fixed what he could.

He never built a clock with one hand.

On certain mornings, when the tide withdrew unusually far, Elias walked across the wet sand to Widow’s Rock. He often found bottles, shells, and driftwood. Once he found a silver buckle that might have come from a wooden leg.

And once, many years later, he found a set of footprints emerging from the sea.

They ended beside a woman in a red coat.

She looked younger than he remembered. Her scar was gone, and her eyes were the blue-gray color of deep water beneath clouds.

“Good morning,” she said.

Elias looked toward the harbor. No white ship waited there.

“Are you collecting something?” he asked.

“Not anymore.”

“What do you want?”

Captain Rook smiled.

“To see what you did with your hour.”

Elias considered this, then offered her his hand.

“Come into town,” he said. “I’ll show you.”

Behind them, the tide began to turn.
